name: Mayappiran Perumal Temple, Thiruppuliyur
deity: Vishnu as Mayappiran (Thrippuliyoorappan), with the Goddess Porkodi Nachiyar
period: A Divya Desam of Malai Nadu (Kerala), sung chiefly by Nammalvar in the Nalayira Divya Prabandham
dynasty: Ancient Malai Nadu shrine of the Chengannur country
summary: At Puliyoor near Chengannur, Vishnu is worshipped as Mayappiran — a Malai Nadu Divya Desam sung by Nammalvar, remembered by tradition as the Pandava Bhima’s shrine and called the Bheemasena Tirupati.

sections.history: Thiruppuliyur, known locally as Puliyoor, lies in Alappuzha district about four kilometres south-west of Chengannur, on the road towards Mavelikara. It is one of the 108 Divya Desams, the abodes of Vishnu sung by the Alvar saints in the Nalayira Divya Prabandham, and belongs to Malai Nadu, the Kerala country. The hymns for this shrine are credited chiefly to Nammalvar, though one source also names Thirumangai Alvar. Its lord is Mayappiran, also invoked as Thrippuliyoorappan, and the Goddess is Porkodi Nachiyar. The temple is counted among the five Pandava-linked Vishnu shrines of the Chengannur country, where tradition assigns Puliyoor to Bhima, the second of the Pandava brothers.
sections.architecture: Puliyoor is a village temple of the Kerala country, set in the quiet green surroundings south-west of Chengannur. The sanctum houses Mayappiran, with the Goddess Porkodi Nachiyar honoured as his consort. The names of its vimana and tank are not firmly recorded; the visitor will find a modest, devotional precinct whose character comes more from its worship and its legends than from monumental scale.
sections.legends: Tradition links this shrine with Bhima, whose strength is the stuff of the Mahabharata; it is sometimes called the Bheemasena Tirupati, and the temple is said to keep Bhima’s mace, the gada. Along with Thrichittatt (Yudhishthira), Aranmula (Arjuna), Thiruvanvandoor (Nakula) and Thrikodithanam (Sahadeva), Puliyoor forms part of the group remembered as the Pancha Pandava temples around Chengannur, each said to have been worshipped by one of the brothers.
sections.festivals: Two annual observances are especially associated with Puliyoor: the arattu festival, the ritual bathing of the deity, held in the month of Dhanu (Margazhi), and the Kavadiattam, the colourful kavadi dance offering, in Makaram (Thai). Vaikunta Ekadashi is also observed here as in other Vaishnava shrines. Dates follow the temple’s calendar, so confirm locally.
sections.experience: A gentle stop on the Pancha Pandava circuit around Chengannur, rewarding for pilgrims who like to follow one story through five villages. Visit unhurried; look for the connection with Bhima that gives the shrine its popular name, and enjoy the village setting. Devotees familiar with Nammalvar’s verses may wish to read them here before darshan.

visit.timings: Open daily with morning and evening darshan sessions, usually with a midday closure; festival days are busiest. Confirm current timings locally before visiting.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional dress is expected — shoulders and knees covered; footwear removed before entering. Follow the posted rules and the priests' guidance.
visit.photography: Photography is restricted in and around the sanctum; follow the posted rules and the priests' guidance.
visit.gettingThere: Puliyoor is about 4 km south-west of Chengannur in Alappuzha district, on the Chengannur–Mavelikara route. Chengannur is the nearest railway station, with autorickshaws, taxis and local buses along the road; Thiruvananthapuram and Kochi are the usual airport gateways.
